## 2. Dense nonlinear reactions can sometimes be fast-forwarded exactly

The interaction skeleton still has a major limitation: its work depends on the number of nonlinear proposals.

A different construction shows that this dependence is not fundamental. There are complex-balanced networks containing only $k$-molecular reactions, for any fixed $k\ge2$, whose exponentially large populations can nevertheless be sampled at arbitrary binary times in polynomial-binary cost.

This is an exact algebraic reduction, not a fluid approximation.



### Collision-completion construction

Take a fixed $d$-state single-molecule generator $A=(a_{ij})$, with positive rational off-diagonal rates and a positive rational stationary vector $c$.

For every $i\ne j$ and every $\beta\in\mathbb Z_+^d$ with $|\beta|=k-1$, introduce


$$e_i+\beta\longrightarrow e_j+\beta$$
with rate constant


$$\kappa_{ij,\beta}
=a_{ij}\binom{k-1}{\beta}.$$
All these reactions conserve the total molecule number $N=\sum_i x_i$. The reaction structure is complex balanced at $c$: each fixed-$\beta$ subnetwork is a translated copy of the balanced single-molecule transition system.

For a single compartment, sum all reactions converting $i$ to $j$:


$$\begin{aligned}
q_{i\to j}(x)
&=\frac{a_{ij}}{V^{k-1}}
\sum_{|\beta|=k-1}
\binom{k-1}{\beta}(x)_{e_i+\beta}\\
&=\boxed{
a_{ij}x_i\frac{(N-1)_{k-1}}{V^{k-1}}.
}
\end{aligned}$$
The second equality is the multivariate falling-factorial Vandermonde identity.

The entire apparently nonlinear population generator is therefore identical to the generator of $N$ independent molecules, each running $A$ with the common time multiplier


$$\alpha_{N,V}=\frac{(N-1)_{k-1}}{V^{k-1}}.$$
Consequently, the exact endpoint law is a convolution of multinomials with row probabilities


$$P_T=\exp(\alpha_{N,V}TA).$$
The accepted finite-generator fast-forwarder computes these probabilities at polynomial binary precision, and the accepted DDB1 binomial calls sample the multinomials without iterating over $N$.

If $N<k$, all reactions are disabled and the algorithm simply returns the initial state.

This gives a complete all-time sampler for this genuinely higher-order family at $n=1$, including very large interaction counts.

## 3. The unrestricted gap survives both constructions

Return to the accepted nonlinear benchmark


$$2A+B\rightleftarrows3A,\qquad
x_0=(2,V-2),\qquad n=1,\quad T=V.$$
Here the corrected independent-family process $Y$ is constant, because there are no source-arity-one reactions.

For this specification,


$$\Lambda=2V,\qquad
\boxed{\Lambda T=2V^2}.$$
Taking $V=2^b$ gives an input of length $O(b)$, while the nonlinear proposal budget is $2^{2b+1}$. The interaction-skeleton algorithm therefore does not meet the required polynomial-binary bound on these inputs.

There is also a sharp discrepancy between global and initial reaction intensities:


$$q_{\mathrm{nonlinear}}(x_0)
=\frac{2(V-2)}{V^2}
\sim\frac2V,$$
whereas the state-independent dominating intensity is $2V$.

Initially, nonlinear events are extremely rare. Following escape from the boundary, nonlinear interactions can become very frequent.

This identifies why a uniform proposal clock loses efficiency: it must cover both extremes, although their relevance to the endpoint is very different.

The accepted result


$$\liminf_{V\to\infty}
\|\mathcal L(X(V))-\pi_\Gamma\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
\ge e^{-2}$$
simultaneously prevents replacing this time window by equilibrium.

Thus this example remains an explicit unresolved case of the original full contract, despite the two additional constructions above.



## 4. What a full algorithm still needs

The strongest remaining direction is not simply faster simulation of individual reactions. It is a method for compressing an evolving nonlinear population law across changes of dynamical scale.

A general construction would have to handle a process which may spend substantial physical time near a boundary, undergo a comparatively rapid nonlinear transition, and subsequently approach equilibrium—all while retaining the correct probability of each outcome.

The accepted stationary product form does not imply that time-dependent distributions remain product-Poisson. Preserving such a form requires additional dynamical conditions, as studied by Anderson, Schnoerr and Yuan. PubMed
